skill.name: x402socks
skill.description: Review live proxy packages and test TLS HTTP CONNECT egress on authorized targets. Purchases use USDC on Base through x402 and require explicit approval.
skill.summary: Review paid TLS proxy quotes, manage access tokens, and verify egress for authorized tests.
skill.author: x402socks

security_audit.summary: Most alerts were documentation syntax, public service URLs, or scoped local checks. Real risks include cleartext legacy options, handling of reusable credentials, disclosure of the direct IP, and gaps in linking approval to purchases and retries. No evidence found of credential harvesting, hidden executable payloads, or prompt injection.

remediation.issue: Approval does not bind the specific purchase request.
remediation.suggestion: Bind a single-use approval to the merchant URL, package, entitlements, signer, exact atomic amount, and payment fields. Recheck all values immediately before signing.

remediation.issue: Retry language can imply permission to sign a second payment.
remediation.suggestion: Reconcile the first authorization and settlement before retrying. Require fresh explicit approval for a new payment, and recover an existing purchase instead of repaying.

remediation.issue: The Python preflight can mistake illustrative values for a user decision.
remediation.suggestion: Require an explicit approval input and move sample values to a non-payment test fixture. Do not let missing approval fall back to example terms.

remediation.issue: Legacy fallback and test overrides can expose reusable credentials.
remediation.suggestion: Remove legacy fallback instructions from agent references. Restrict insecure testing to loopback with synthetic credentials and exact production hosts for live credential requests.

remediation.issue: Manual snippets bypass the helper and persist sensitive material.
remediation.suggestion: Use the checked helper, or apply equivalent private-file and curl safeguards. Keep recovery proofs out of persistent files and disable shell tracing around credentials.

remediation.issue: Quote output can misrepresent budget compliance.
remediation.suggestion: Require HTTP 402 and one well-formed requirement. Parse the cap and amount as finite integer atomic USDC values and report when no cap is configured.

remediation.issue: Token file checks and opening are separate operations.
remediation.suggestion: Open the token without following symlinks from a trusted directory descriptor. Verify file type, owner, permissions, and size on the same descriptor before reading.

remediation.issue: Provider output and address diagnostics can disclose more than needed.
remediation.suggestion: Allowlist nonsecret output fields and omit full IP addresses by default. Disclose the independent IP service and ask before performing the direct baseline test.

remediation.issue: Client snippets do not enforce authorized destinations.
remediation.suggestion: Restrict automated integrations to operator-approved destinations and stop when a target denies automated access. Do not retry a denied request through another exit.

semantic_findings.title: Payment Approval Does Not Bind the Package or Request
semantic_findings.description: The TypeScript guard verifies payment terms but uses a fixed purchase URL. It cannot establish that the signed payment buys the package or entitlements the user approved.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The matcher checks financial fields but does not receive the request URL or package ID. The purchase URL is a literal in the example.

semantic_findings.title: Quote Budget Check Can Give False Assurance
semantic_findings.description: The quote checks for a payment header but not HTTP status. The optional floating-point cap can accept a non-finite input and report that the quote is within budget.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The status code is not checked. The cap is parsed as a float without a finiteness check, and the quote path does not sign.

semantic_findings.title: Python Review Example Uses Sample Terms as Approval
semantic_findings.description: The Python example labels hardcoded sample values as approved terms. A copied integration can pass the preflight without obtaining a user decision, although the example itself does not sign.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The example initializes the approval from literals and checks the challenge against them. Its comments require replacing them, but the executable preflight does not enforce that requirement.

semantic_findings.title: Retry Guidance Does Not Require Fresh Payment Approval
semantic_findings.description: The troubleshooting guide suggests re-signing after another 402 and considering a new purchase after connection failures. It does not consistently require reconciling the first authorization or obtaining new approval.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The retry guidance says to re-sign, while the main skill demands approval before spending. A separate stop rule for second packages reduces but does not remove the ambiguity.

semantic_findings.title: Manual Curl Examples Bypass Credential Safeguards
semantic_findings.description: Manual status and proxy requests inherit settings from the user's default curl configuration. Custom tracing or output settings can expose authentication data even when the destination uses TLS.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The documented invocations do not disable the default curl configuration. The helper explicitly disables it; no hostile local configuration was observed.

semantic_findings.title: Token File Checks Are Separate From the File Open
semantic_findings.description: The reader checks the path and then reopens it by name. If another process can replace the entry, the reader may use bytes from a file it never verified.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The mode and owner checks precede a separate open. The issue requires local control of the relevant path and is not observed under normal private-directory use.

semantic_findings.title: Credential Responses Are Not Output-Allowlisted
semantic_findings.description: Status prints the provider response. Rotation and recovery redact only the top-level token field, leaving account details and any additional sensitive response fields visible to the calling agent.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The output paths do not filter fields beyond the replacement token. No evidence found that current vendor responses include a second secret.

semantic_findings.title: Authorized-Target Boundary Depends on the Operator
semantic_findings.description: The skill advertises rotating and regional egress. Client examples provide general proxy access, so the user's authorization and the target's access rules are not enforced by the integration.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The browser example configures the proxy but does not restrict destinations. The documentation requires authorization and says to stop at site bans; no abusive use was observed.

content.user_title: Quote and Test TLS Proxy Access
content.value_statement: Testing a service from another region requires knowing the price, transport, and available exits. This skill checks those details and guides approved purchases and egress tests.
actual_capabilities: Checks service health and lists exits marked healthy and enabled by the provider.
Lists catalog prices and entitlements and reads live payment terms without signing.
Documents TypeScript and Python checks for comparing one live payment option with approved terms.
Stores a proxy token locally and supports status checks, validation, rotation, and recovery.
Tests TLS proxy egress by comparing it with a direct baseline using an external IP reporting service.
limitations: Purchases require a funded Base USDC wallet, a compatible signer, and explicit approval. The shell helper does not buy packages.
The helper requires curl and Python for most operations. It does not expose legacy SOCKS5 or plaintext proxy transports.
Exit health, package terms, and session limits can change. A different IP does not prove anonymity or target availability.
The egress test sends a direct request to an IP reporting service. A valid proxy token is required.

use_cases.title: Plan a Regional QA Check
use_cases.description: Review available TLS exits before scheduling a test against a staging service you control.

use_cases.title: Review a Proxy Purchase Request
use_cases.description: Compare a live quote with the catalog and record the exact terms for a human decision.

use_cases.title: Diagnose a Proxy Incident
use_cases.description: Separate a service outage, an unavailable exit, and an invalid token without initiating a new purchase.

prompt_templates.title: Beginner: Check Service Health
prompt_templates.prompt: Check the provider health and summarize the enabled, healthy exits. Do not read credentials, test egress, or make a purchase.

prompt_templates.title: Intermediate: Review a Quote
prompt_templates.prompt: Compare a live unsigned quote for [package] with the public catalog. Show the exact charge, recipient, network, asset, and entitlements. Do not sign or pay.

prompt_templates.title: Practitioner: Triage a Failed Connection
prompt_templates.scenario: Diagnose an incident from sanitized evidence
prompt_templates.prompt: Use these sanitized errors to distinguish a token issue, an exit issue, and a problem with our staging service. Do not rotate credentials or buy access.

prompt_templates.title: Advanced: Check Approval Consistency
prompt_templates.prompt: Compare these redacted challenge terms with [approval]. Flag any differences in the package, merchant URL, recipient, network, asset, domain, or atomic amount. Do not sign.

output_examples.input: Review this sample quote for a six-hour package without paying.
output_examples.output: The sample offers six hours, up to 1 GB, and one active session. The challenge lists 1 USDC on Base. No payment was signed or sent.

output_examples.input: Interpret this sample provisioning error after payment.
output_examples.output: The provider reports that settlement succeeded but provisioning failed. Verify settlement using the transaction hash. Review recovery options before considering any new payment.

output_examples.input: Summarize these sanitized exit and token checks.
output_examples.output: The provider marked the exit healthy. Token validation returned an authentication error. Check whether the token expired or was rotated. No secret was displayed.

best_practices: Use TLS CONNECT only and keep real tokens in a private file. Keep tokens and signing material out of chat and logs.
Verify the live package, merchant destination, and exact terms with a person before signing. Stop when terms differ.
Use only authorized destinations. Confirm who receives diagnostic traffic before comparing direct and proxy egress.
anti_patterns: Treating a spending cap or a prior quote as approval for a new charge.
Switching to plaintext or disabling certificate verification when TLS fails.
Buying again after an uncertain settlement or trying another exit to bypass a target's denial.

faq.question: Can I check prices without a wallet?
faq.answer: Yes. Catalog lookups and unsigned quotes do not require a wallet. A purchase requires a compatible signer and USDC on Base.

faq.question: Does the helper automatically buy access?
faq.answer: No. It reads quotes and manages proxy credentials. Signing a purchase requires a separate client or signer and explicit approval.

faq.question: Does the helper use SOCKS5?
faq.answer: No. The helper uses TLS HTTP CONNECT. Legacy transports documented for browsers do not protect the token on the client-to-proxy hop.

faq.question: What happens if a proxy token is lost?
faq.answer: A recoverable purchase can use its settlement transaction and a proof from the paying wallet. Check settlement before considering another purchase.

faq.question: Does an egress change prove anonymity?
faq.answer: No. It only shows that the test saw a different public IP. The test also contacts an external service directly to establish the baseline.

faq.question: How can I use this with an AI client?
faq.answer: Use a client with shell execution and the required tools. Without shell access, the references can still support a read-only review.
